yaml.title: Why Every Developer Should Write
yaml.description: Writing sharpens thinking. Here is why developers should blog more.
yaml.author: Your Name

markdown.markdown:
Most developers I know are extraordinarily good at thinking in systems—at decomposing problems,
spotting edge cases, and reasoning about trade-offs. Yet the same people often tell me they
"can't write." I think they've confused *polish* with *clarity*, and that's a fixable mistake.

---


When you write, you're not transcribing thoughts that are already finished. You're *discovering*
what you actually think. The discipline of forming a sentence forces you to choose between
ideas, discard the weak ones, and commit to the strong ones.

![A developer writing at a desk](thumbnail.png){fig-alt="Developer writing at a desk" fig-align="center" width="80%"}

> "I write to find out what I think."
>
> — Joan Didion

---

## Five Reasons Developers Should Blog

1. **Teaching solidifies understanding.** The "Feynman technique"—explain a concept simply until
   you can't—exposes every gap in your knowledge faster than any test.
2. **Your future self will thank you.** A post explaining how you solved a tricky CORS issue is a
   personal reference you'll return to, and it'll save someone else three hours of debugging.
3. **Writing compounds.** Thirty posts means thirty permanent search-indexed artifacts of your
   expertise. That's a form of leverage most developers ignore entirely.
4. **It builds professional credibility.** Recruiters, hiring managers, and peers read blogs.
   A thoughtful post demonstrates judgment in a way a résumé cannot.
5. **It builds the habit of finishing things.** A blog post has a clear done state. That's
   rarer and more valuable than it sounds.

---

## Common Objections (and Why They Don't Hold)

**"I don't have anything original to say."** You don't need to be first. You need to be *useful*.
A beginner's explanation of a hard topic is often more helpful than the expert's, because you
remember what confused you.

**"No one will read it."** Write for one person: your past self, six months ago. If it would
have helped you then, publish it.

**"I don't have time."** A 400-word post once a month is better than nothing. Write rough. Edit
once. Ship.

---

## How to Start

The tooling friction is lower than ever:

- [Quarto](https://quarto.org) — code-friendly, renders to HTML, PDF, or slides from one source
- [Ghost](https://ghost.org) — beautifully minimal hosted blogging
- [Obsidian Publish](https://obsidian.md/publish) — if you already live in Obsidian

Pick whichever puts the least distance between you and the publish button. The best tool is the
one you'll actually use.

> "Amateurs sit and wait for inspiration. The rest of us just show up and get to work."
>
> — Stephen King, *On Writing*

<script>
window.addEventListener('scroll', function() {
  const btn = document.getElementById('quarto-back-to-top');
  if (!btn) return;

  const scrollPos = window.scrollY;
  const totalHeight = document.documentElement.scrollHeight;
  const viewportHeight = window.innerHeight;
  const bottomThreshold = 15;

  if (scrollPos <= 0 || (scrollPos + viewportHeight >= totalHeight - bottomThreshold)) {
    btn.style.setProperty('display', 'none', 'important');
  } else if (scrollPos > 100) {
    btn.style.setProperty('display', 'block', 'important');
  }
});

document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function() {
  const currentUrl = window.location.href.toLowerCase();
  const navLinks = document.querySelectorAll('.navbar-nav .nav-link');
  
  if (currentUrl.includes('/articles/') || currentUrl.includes('\\articles\\') || currentUrl.endsWith('articles/')) {
    navLinks.forEach(link => {
      if (link.innerText.trim() === 'Articles') {
        link.classList.add('active');
      } else if (link.innerText.trim() === 'Home' || link.innerText.trim() === 'About') {
        link.classList.remove('active');
      }
    });
  }
});
</script>
